passage: Simran, last Saturday you said, "Mum is impatient, Papa forgets things, and they're better apart. I have my own exams." I noticed you weren't angry when you said it, and I was glad. I'm Rekha, your Nani, and I'll tell you about my own parents, who separated when I was sixteen. I was calm very quickly. Too quickly. I told everyone I understood, and by nineteen it all crashed out in a college hostel corridor, over nothing. What I learnt was that calm needs some crying before it. You seem to have done yours. Keep visiting both houses, and tell them honestly how you are. And if the sadness returns, let it. It doesn't mean you took a step back.

qa.q: How old was Rekha when her parents separated?
What does Simran's calm remark about Mum and Papa suggest about how Simran now sees them?
qa.a: Simran seems to see them as imperfect people who do better apart and to focus on Simran's own life, without anger.

qa.q: What advice does Rekha give Simran about handling the family from here?
qa.a: To keep visiting both houses, be honest with each parent about how Simran feels, and let sadness come back if it does.

qa.q: How does Rekha's own story differ from Simran's situation?
qa.a: Rekha became calm too quickly without grieving and it crashed out at nineteen, while Simran seems to have cried first, so Simran's calm looks steadier.

grounding: Shows a teen who has come to see both divorcing parents as flawed people better apart, with an elder warning against forcing calm before grieving.

passage:
Two years ago, when Papa moved to Hyderabad, I was the calmest person in our house. Everyone said how mature I was. Actually I was holding my breath. Six months later I snapped at my friend Neelam over nothing and sobbed in the school washroom for an hour. That was when the grief finally came.
It took a long time. Now, at seventeen, I can see them both more clearly. Mummy is stubborn and brave. Papa is funny and bad at listening. Together, they were always tired. Apart, they are kinder people.
I visit Papa every second weekend. When his new flat felt strange, I told him so instead of pretending. I've also started planning my own things: the college fair, my swimming. My life isn't only about their split anymore.
Neelam said last week, "You seem lighter, Kalyani." I think I am.

qa.q: Where did Papa move two years ago?
What was Kalyani feeling when everyone called Kalyani mature?
qa.a: Kalyani was not calm at all, only holding back grief, which broke out months later in sobbing in the school washroom.

qa.q: What is working in how Kalyani handles things now?
qa.a: Kalyani visits Papa regularly, tells both parents honestly how things feel, and puts energy into college plans and swimming.

qa.q: How might Neelam see the change in Kalyani?
qa.a: Neelam seems relieved and glad, noticing that Kalyani seems lighter after the time Neelam was snapped at for nothing.

grounding: A teen looks back on forcing calm too early, grieving later, and coming to accept both parents as flawed people who do better apart.

passage:
Coach's note, under-18 hockey, 14 March
Parul arrived early today and stayed after practice to help the juniors, as she has most weeks this term. Last autumn she missed games and snapped at teammates when her parents were separating. Her younger brother Tejas, who plays in the under-12 squad, told me then that home was "very loud."
Today, while we packed cones, she told me plainly that her parents are happier living apart. She is at her father's place on Saturdays and her mother's the rest of the week, and she arranges her match schedule around both. She said she tells them honestly when a weekend feels hard.
I asked whether she still feels sad. She paused, then said, "Sometimes, yes. I let it be sad now." That sounded honest, not forced.
Next step: I'll keep up our Friday check-ins and let the school counsellor know she's doing well.

qa.q: Which day is Parul at her father's place?
What does Parul's pause before answering suggest about her feelings?
qa.a: It suggests she still feels some sadness but has made peace with it; she allows herself to feel sad instead of forcing calm.

qa.q: How is the adult who wrote the note supporting Parul?
qa.a: By noticing the change, asking gently about sadness, keeping weekly check-ins and sharing the good news with the school counsellor.

qa.q: How might Tejas experience this change at home?
qa.a: Tejas described home as very loud last autumn, so a calmer sister and quieter homes may feel like a relief to Tejas as well.

grounding: A teen, observed by a coach, has come to accept her parents' separation, stays honest with both, and runs her own life.
